findings.message:
Integer Overflow/Underflow Identified.

1. Integer Underflow in `MathUtils.difference`
'''
The `difference` function is implemented inside an `unchecked` block, but it does not return after the `if (a > b)` branch. When `a > b`, it first sets `diff = a - b`, then unconditionally executes `diff = b - a`, which underflows because `b < a`. As a result, `difference(a, b)` returns a huge incorrect value whenever `a > b`. This breaks `within1`, which is used in the invariant/convergence checks in `_computeLiquidityFromAdjustedBalances` and `_getY`, potentially causing incorrect swap/mint/burn calculations and denial-of-service.

Recommended fix:
```solidity
function difference(uint256 a, uint256 b) internal pure returns (uint256 diff) {
    unchecked {
        return a > b ? a - b : b - a;
    }
}
```
'''

2. Integer Underflow in `TridentERC20.transfer`
'''
The `transfer` function performs:
```solidity
balanceOf[msg.sender] -= amount;
```
inside an `unchecked` block. If `amount` exceeds the caller’s balance, the subtraction does not revert; instead, `balanceOf[msg.sender]` wraps to a huge value. This breaks the ERC-20 accounting invariant and lets an attacker effectively mint unlimited balance to themselves, which can be used to steal funds from the pool or other
Detector: ArithmeticDetector
Classification: SWC-101, DASP-3
findings.name: Integer Overflow / Underflow

findings.message:
Unchecked External Calls Identified.

VULNERABILITY NAME or TYPE
'''
Unchecked Low-Level Staticcalls
'''
The contract performs multiple low-level `staticcall` operations while discarding the returned success boolean. This occurs in the constructor when querying `barFee`, `barFeeTo`, `bento`, and token `decimals()`, as well as in the internal helper functions `__balance`, `_toAmount`, `_toShare`, and in `updateBarFee`. For example:

```solidity
(, bytes memory _barFee) = _masterDeployer.staticcall(...);
(, bytes memory _decimals0) = _token0.staticcall(...);
(, bytes memory ___balance) = bento.staticcall(...);
```

In each case the first return value, which indicates whether the external call succeeded, is not checked. If the external contract reverts, the returned bytes will be empty and the subsequent `abi.decode` will typically revert. However, this is not guaranteed in all edge cases, and the contract is also relying on revert-during-decode rather than explicitly handling a failed call. This can lead to unexpected reverts, denial-of-service during initialization, or incorrect behavior if the called contract returns malformed or unexpected data.

RECOMMENDED MITIGATION: Always capture and validate the success boolean for every low-level `call`, `staticcall`, and `delegatecall`. For example:

```solidity
(bool success, bytes memory data) = target.staticcall(...);
require(success, "External call failed");
```

Only after verifying `success` should the returned data be decoded. Apply this pattern to all staticcalls in the constructor, `__balance`, `_toAmount`, `_toShare`, and `updateBarFee`.

VULNERABILITY NAME or TYPE
'''
Unchecked Callback External Call
'''
In `_processSwap`, the contract invokes `ITridentCallee(msg.sender).tridentSwapCallback(data)` without verifying that the external call actually executed. Because `msg.sender` is supplied by the caller, it may be an EOA or a contract that does not implement the callback. Solidity high-level calls to an address with no code will succeed without executing anything, so this callback can be silently skipped. While the subsequent “amount in” balance checks in `flashSwap` may still prevent theft, the callback itself is an unchecked external interaction and may cause inconsistencies or bypass expected protocol behavior in more complex integrations.

RECOMMENDED MITIGATION: Verify the success of the callback call, or explicitly check that `msg.sender` is a contract with the expected callback implementation before invoking it. Using a low-level call and requiring its success is safer:

```solidity
(bool success, ) = msg.sender.call(abi.encodeWithSelector(ITridentCallee.tridentSwapCallback.selector, data));
require(success, "Callback failed");
```

This ensures that the callback either runs successfully or the entire transaction reverts.
'''
Detector: UncheckedSendDetector
Classification: SWC-104, DASP-4
findings.name: Unchecked External Call (send/transfer/ERC20 return)

findings.message:
Unchecked Low-level Calls Identified.

VULNERABILITY NAME or TYPE
'''
Unchecked Low-Level Staticcall Return Values
'''
DETAILED DESCRIPTION:
The contract performs multiple low-level `staticcall` operations while discarding the returned success boolean. This occurs in the constructor when fetching `barFee`, `barFeeTo`, `bento`, and token `decimals()`, as well as in the internal functions `__balance`, `_toAmount`, `_toShare`, and in `updateBarFee()`. For instance:

```solidity
(, bytes memory _barFee) = _masterDeployer.staticcall(...);
(, bytes memory _decimals0) = _token0.staticcall(...);
(, bytes memory ___balance) = bento.staticcall(...);
```

The first tuple element is the success flag, but it is always ignored. If the external call fails, the returned bytes will be empty and `abi.decode` may revert. However, relying on decode failure is not a robust error-handling pattern. More importantly, if the called contract returns malformed, unexpected, or maliciously crafted data that still decodes successfully, the contract may use incorrect values without any indication that the external call was not successful. This can lead to incorrect reserve calculations, denial-of-service during deployment, or protocol misbehavior.

RECOMMENDED MITIGATION:
For every low-level `staticcall`, capture the success boolean and validate it before decoding the returned data. Revert explicitly if the call fails. Apply this pattern consistently to all staticcalls in the constructor, `__balance`, `_toAmount`, `_toShare`, and `updateBarFee`.

```solidity
(bool success, bytes memory data) = target.staticcall(...);
require(success, "External call failed");
```

Only after verifying `success` should the returned bytes be decoded. This ensures that failed external queries are handled deterministically and the contract does not continue with invalid or empty data.

VULNERABILITY NAME or TYPE
'''
Unchecked Callback External Call in `_processSwap`
'''
DETAILED DESCRIPTION:
In `_processSwap`, the contract invokes the external callback:

```solidity
if (data.length != 0) ITridentCallee(msg.sender).tridentSwapCallback(data);
```

This is a high-level external call whose return value is not checked. If `msg.sender` is an EOA or a contract that does not implement `tridentSwapCallback`, the call may silently succeed without executing any callback logic. Solidity treats calls to accounts without code as successful, so the callback can be silently skipped. While the balance checks in `flashSwap` may still prevent funds from being lost, this unchecked interaction can create inconsistencies, allow integrations to behave differently than expected, and generally violates the principle of verifying all external call results.

RECOMMENDED MITIGATION:
Verify that the callback call actually succeeded, or explicitly ensure that `msg.sender` is a contract implementing the expected callback interface. Use a low-level call and require its success so that a missing or failing callback causes the entire transaction to revert:

```solidity
(bool success, ) = msg.sender.call(
    abi.encodeWithSelector(ITridentCallee.tridentSwapCallback.selector, data)
);
require(success, "Callback failed");
```

Alternatively, check that `msg.sender.code.length > 0` and that it implements the callback before invocation. This prevents silent callback failures and makes external interactions safer and more predictable.
'''
Detector: UncheckedLowLevelCallDetector
Classification: SWC-104, DASP-4
findings.name: Unchecked Low-level Call (call/delegatecall/send)

findings.message:
Redundant Conditional Check Identified.

Redundant Conditional Check – MathUtils.difference()
'''
The conditional `if (a > b)` inside `MathUtils.difference()` is redundant and ineffective. When `a > b`, the function first assigns `diff = a - b`, but then unconditionally executes `diff = b - a`, overwriting the previous value. Since the branch result is always discarded, the condition does not affect the outcome and only adds unnecessary complexity and gas cost. Moreover, because the calculation is in an `unchecked` block, `b - a` underflows for `a > b`, producing an incorrect and misleading result. The function should be corrected to return the true absolute difference, for example by returning `a - b` when `a > b` and `b - a` otherwise, instead of falling through to a second assignment.
'''

Redundant Conditional Check – _computeLiquidityFromAdjustedBalances()
'''
The conditional `if (s == 0) { computed = 0; }` in `_computeLiquidityFromAdjustedBalances()` is redundant because it does not prevent execution from continuing into the iterative loop. The assignment `computed = 0` is immediately overwritten by the subsequent `computed = D` logic, and when `s == 0`, both `xp0` and `xp1` are zero, so the loop attempts a division by zero and reverts. The zero-balance case should be handled with an early return or another explicit guard before the loop, ensuring the conditional actually changes control flow and avoids the invalid computation.
'''
Detector: RedundantConditionalDetector
Classification: code-quality (no standard SWC)
findings.name: Redundant Conditional Check

findings.message:
Centralization Risk Identified.

CENTRALIZED CONTROL OF PROTOCOL FEE PARAMETERS
'''
The `HybridPool` contract does not have owner-only functions, but it centralizes fee-related control through the external `masterDeployer` and the immutable `barFeeTo` address. At construction, `barFee`, `barFeeTo`, and `bento` are read from `masterDeployer`. The `barFeeTo` address is stored as immutable, so it can never be changed for a deployed pool. Meanwhile, `updateBarFee()` lets anyone sync the `barFee` value from `masterDeployer`, meaning the actual protocol fee rate is entirely controlled by the `masterDeployer` contract. If `masterDeployer` or `barFeeTo` is a single EOA or compromised account, it can arbitrarily set the fee rate and receive protocol fees with no timelock, multisig, or on-chain governance. This creates a single point of trust and centralization risk.

Mitigation: Use a decentralized governance mechanism such as a DAO, TimelockController, or multisig wallet for `masterDeployer` and `barFeeTo`. Additionally, enforce a maximum fee cap inside the pool and make any `barFee` change subject to a timelock so that users and LPs have time to react.
'''

CENTRALIZED EXTRACTION OF FLASH-SWAP FEES
'''
In `flashSwap()`, the entire `swapFee` is transferred to `barFeeTo` via `_transfer(tokenIn, fee, barFeeTo, false)`. This differs from the normal `swap()` path, where `_handleFee()` transfers only the `barFee` portion to `barFeeTo` and leaves the rest of the fee in the pool for LPs. As written, every flash swap sends 100% of the swap fee to the single centralized `barFeeTo` address, bypassing the LP fee-sharing mechanism. This amplifies the centralization risk because a compromised or malicious `barFeeTo` receives not only the protocol cut but also the liquidity providers’ expected fee share.

Mitigation: In `flashSwap()`, use the same fee-splitting logic as `swap()` — send only `(fee * barFee) / MAX_FEE` to `barFeeTo` and retain the remaining fee in the pool for LPs. The `barFeeTo` address should also be controlled by a decentralized governance mechanism rather than a single party.
'''
Detector: CentralizationRiskDetector
Classification: DASP-2 / governance (no standard SWC)
findings.name: Centralization Risk
